subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Anovulatory infertility, PCOS, ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic amenorrhea
vignette: A couple presents for evaluation of infertility. The wife has irregular menstrual cycles and mid-luteal progesterone testing confirms that she is not ovulating. The physician reviews the recognized causes of anovulatory infertility.
question: Which of the following is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility?

options.text: Polycystic ovary syndrome
Primary ovarian insufficiency
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism
Hyperprolactinemia
Imperforate hymen

explanation_correct: Polycystic ovary syndrome is the most common cause of anovulatory infertility. Other causes include primary ovarian insufficiency, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hyperprolactinemia. Anovulation is physiologically normal during pregnancy, breastfeeding, and around menarche and menopause, so those states are not considered pathologic.

explanation_incorrect.B: Primary ovarian insufficiency is a recognized cause of anovulation but is less common than PCOS.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism can cause anovulation but is not the most common cause.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hyperprolactinemia is a cause of anovulatory infertility but occurs less frequently than PCOS.
explanation_incorrect.E: Imperforate hymen causes primary amenorrhea and hematocolpos from an anatomic outflow obstruction, not anovulation.

educationalObjective: Anovulatory infertility causes include PCOS (most common), primary ovarian insufficiency, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and hyperprolactinemia; anovulation is normal in pregnancy, breastfeeding, near menarche/menopause.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Anovulatory infertility, PCOS, ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic amenorrhea
vignette: A 26-year-old woman has oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, and a BMI of 32. Pelvic ultrasound shows enlarged ovaries with multiple peripheral follicles. Laboratory testing shows an elevated LH:FSH ratio and increased testosterone.
question: Which of the following best explains the development of anovulation in this patient?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of ovarian follicles causing Low estrogen and elevated FSH
Excess prolactin suppressing GnRH pulsatility
A pituitary adenoma secreting excess FSH causing ovarian hyperstimulation
Increased LH stimulation of theca interna cells with reduced follicular maturation
Aromatase deficiency preventing conversion of androgens to estrogens

explanation_correct: In PCOS, dysregulated ovarian steroidogenesis produces an increased LH:FSH ratio. Excess LH stimulates theca interna cells to produce androgens, while the relatively low FSH reduces the rate of follicular maturation. The result is unruptured follicles (cysts) and anovulation, along with hyperandrogenism and insulin resistance.

explanation_incorrect.A: Autoimmune oophoritis causes primary ovarian insufficiency with low estrogen and elevated FSH, not the elevated LH:FSH ratio and hyperandrogenism of PCOS.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hyperprolactinemia is a distinct cause of anovulation and would present with galactorrhea rather than hirsutism and cystic ovaries.
explanation_incorrect.C: PCOS features an increased LH:FSH ratio, not excess FSH secretion from a pituitary adenoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Aromatase deficiency is a separate disorder and is not the mechanism underlying PCOS.

educationalObjective: PCOS: dysregulated steroidogenesis with increased LH:FSH leads to increased theca interna androgens and reduced follicular maturation, causing cysts and anovulation.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Anovulatory infertility, PCOS, ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic amenorrhea
vignette: A 24-year-old woman is evaluated for irregular periods and mild hirsutism. Pelvic ultrasound shows cystic/enlarged ovaries, and laboratory testing shows mildly elevated testosterone. Her physician applies the accepted diagnostic criteria for PCOS.
question: Which of the following best reflects the diagnostic criteria for PCOS in this patient?

options.text: All three features—oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and cystic ovaries—must be present.
At least two of the following: oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, and cystic/enlarged ovaries.
Cystic ovaries plus insulin resistance are required in every case.
An elevated LH:FSH ratio alone is sufficient for the diagnosis.
The presence of acanthosis nigricans is required for the diagnosis.

explanation_correct: PCOS is diagnosed when at least two of three features are present: cystic/enlarged ovaries on ultrasound, oligo-/anovulation, and hyperandrogenism (eg, hirsutism or acne). This patient has oligomenorrhea, hirsutism with elevated testosterone, and cystic ovaries, easily satisfying the criteria. Insulin resistance, obesity, and acanthosis nigricans are associations but are not required.

explanation_incorrect.A: Only two of the three features are required; all three are not mandatory for diagnosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Insulin resistance and acanthosis nigricans are common associations but are not required diagnostic criteria.
explanation_incorrect.D: An elevated LH:FSH ratio supports the diagnosis but is not itself one of the formal diagnostic criteria.
explanation_incorrect.E: Acanthosis nigricans is an associated finding reflecting insulin resistance, not a required criterion.

educationalObjective: PCOS is diagnosed with at least two of: cystic/enlarged ovaries, oligo/anovulation, and hyperandrogenism (hirsutism/acne).

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Anovulatory infertility, PCOS, ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic amenorrhea
vignette: A 38-year-old woman with PCOS has gone months without a menstrual period. She is obese, insulin resistant, and has acanthosis nigricans. Her physician explains that her repeated anovulatory cycles increase her risk for a specific malignancy and reviews management options.
question: Which of the following best explains her increased cancer risk and an appropriate intervention?

options.text: Unopposed estrogen from intermittent ovulation raises ovarian cancer risk; treat with metformin alone.
Unopposed progesterone raises cervical cancer risk; give cyclic progestin only.
Unopposed estrogen from anovulatory cycles raises endometrial cancer risk; give OCPs to prevent endometrial hyperplasia.
Excess androgens directly cause vulvar carcinoma; give spironolactone.
Hyperinsulinemia causes breast cancer; recommend weight gain.

explanation_correct: In PCOS, repeated anovulatory cycles mean the endometrium is exposed to estrogen without the opposing effect of progesterone from ovulation. This unopposed estrogen increases the risk of endometrial hyperplasia and endometrial cancer. Oral contraceptives regulate cycles and protect the endometrium; weight loss reduces peripheral estrone formation, and ovulation induction is used for infertility.

explanation_incorrect.A: The classic malignancy risk in PCOS is endometrial, not ovarian, and metformin alone does not provide endometrial protection.
explanation_incorrect.B: The problem is unopposed estrogen rather than progesterone, and the target organ is the endometrium, not the cervix.
explanation_incorrect.D: Excess androgens cause hirsutism and acne, not vulvar carcinoma; spironolactone treats hirsutism but does not address the cancer risk.
explanation_incorrect.E: Weight loss, not weight gain, is recommended in PCOS, and the characteristic cancer risk is endometrial rather than breast.

educationalObjective: In PCOS, unopposed estrogen from anovulatory cycles increases endometrial cancer risk; OCPs prevent hyperplasia, while weight loss, ovulation induction, and antiandrogens are also used.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Anovulatory infertility, PCOS, ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic amenorrhea
vignette: A 36-year-old woman has not menstruated for 8 months and has hot flashes and vaginal dryness. She had normal puberty and regular menses in her 20s. Laboratory studies show estradiol 12 pg/mL, FSH 78 mIU/mL, and LH 65 mIU/mL. One of her sisters has fragile X syndrome.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and the appropriate associated evaluation?

options.text: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea; no genetic testing is needed
PCOS; pelvic ultrasound alone is diagnostic
Hyperprolactinemia; check a prolactin level only
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; check a GnRH level
Primary ovarian insufficiency; obtain a karyotype and evaluate for a fragile X premutation

explanation_correct: Primary ovarian insufficiency (premature ovarian failure) is premature atresia of ovarian follicles before age 40, producing menopausal signs after puberty with low estrogen and elevated LH and FSH. It is often idiopathic but is associated with Turner syndrome, fragile X premutation, and autoimmunity, so karyotype screening is indicated. The elevated gonadotropins distinguish it from hypothalamic causes.

explanation_incorrect.A: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea features low LH and FSH, not the markedly elevated gonadotropins seen in this patient.
explanation_incorrect.B: PCOS features hyperandrogenism and cystic ovaries with normal or elevated LH but not the high FSH of ovarian failure.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hyperprolactinemia would not produce FSH this high and would be evaluated with a prolactin level rather than karyotype.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism features low LH and FSH; here gonadotropins are high, indicating primary ovarian failure.

educationalObjective: Primary ovarian insufficiency: premature follicle atresia before 40 with decreased estrogen and increased LH/FSH; associated with Turner, fragile X premutation, autoimmunity—obtain karyotype.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Anovulatory infertility, PCOS, ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic amenorrhea
vignette: A 19-year-old college athlete trains intensely and severely restricts her calories. She has had no menstrual periods for 7 months, has lost bone mineral density, and is very thin. Laboratory testing shows low LH, low FSH, and low estradiol.
question: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of her amenorrhea?

options.text: Premature atresia of ovarian follicles causing elevated FSH
Stress and low energy availability disrupt pulsatile GnRH, lowering LH, FSH, and estrogen
Excess prolactin from a pituitary adenoma suppressing ovulation
Increased leptin from high body fat suppressing GnRH
Androgen excess from theca interna cells causing anovulation

explanation_correct: Functional (exercise-induced) hypothalamic amenorrhea results from severe caloric restriction, increased energy expenditure, and stress, which functionally disrupt pulsatile GnRH secretion, lowering LH, FSH, and estrogen. Pathogenesis includes decreased leptin from low fat mass and increased cortisol. It is associated with eating disorders and the female athlete triad of low energy availability, low bone mineral density, and menstrual dysfunction.

explanation_incorrect.A: Follicular atresia with elevated FSH is primary ovarian insufficiency, not hypothalamic amenorrhea, in which gonadotropins are low.
explanation_incorrect.C: Hyperprolactinemia is a separate cause and would typically feature galactorrhea, not the calorie restriction and exercise history described.
explanation_incorrect.D: Leptin is decreased because of low fat mass, not increased, in functional hypothalamic amenorrhea.
explanation_incorrect.E: Androgen excess from theca interna cells is the mechanism of PCOS, which would show hyperandrogenism rather than low gonadotropins.

educationalObjective: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhea: severe caloric restriction/excess exercise/stress disrupt pulsatile GnRH, lowering LH/FSH/estrogen, with decreased leptin and increased cortisol; part of the female athlete triad.

subject: Reproductive
subtopic: Anovulatory infertility, PCOS, ovarian insufficiency, hypothalamic amenorrhea
vignette: A 30-year-old woman has amenorrhea and galactorrhea. MRI shows a small pituitary lesion, and her prolactin is markedly elevated while estrogen is low. The physician explains how excess prolactin leads to her anovulation.
question: Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which hyperprolactinemia causes anovulation in this patient?

options.text: Prolactin directly destroys ovarian follicles, raising FSH and lowering estrogen.
Prolactin stimulates theca interna cells to overproduce androgens, as in PCOS.
Prolactin increases adipose aromatase activity, converting androgens to estrone.
Prolactin suppresses pulsatile GnRH secretion, lowering LH and FSH and thus estrogen.
Prolactin blocks the endometrial estrogen receptor, preventing menstruation despite normal ovulatory cycles.

explanation_correct: Hyperprolactinemia causes anovulation by suppressing pulsatile GnRH secretion from the hypothalamus, which lowers LH and FSH and consequently reduces estrogen production. This presents with amenorrhea and galactorrhea. The mechanism is central suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis rather than a direct ovarian effect.

explanation_incorrect.A: Prolactin does not destroy ovarian follicles; in hyperprolactinemic anovulation gonadotropins are low, not elevated.
explanation_incorrect.B: Theca interna androgen excess is the mechanism of PCOS, not hyperprolactinemia, and would produce hirsutism rather than galactorrhea.
explanation_incorrect.C: Aromatase conversion of androgens to estrone in adipose tissue occurs in PCOS and obesity but is not driven by prolactin.
explanation_incorrect.E: Prolactin acts centrally to suppress GnRH, not by blocking the endometrial estrogen receptor; ovulation itself is suppressed.

educationalObjective: Hyperprolactinemia causes anovulation by suppressing pulsatile GnRH, lowering LH/FSH and estrogen, presenting with amenorrhea and galactorrhea.
